overview.title: Iterated K-fold, common-sense baselines, and evaluation pitfalls
overview.subsection: 5.2.3 Things to keep in mind about model evaluation
overview.main_topic: The third evaluation protocol (iterated K-fold with shuffling), the need to beat a trivial baseline, and the start of the checklist of evaluation pitfalls
overview.central_idea: When data is scarce and precision matters, repeat K-fold P times with reshuffling and average (P x K models). Whatever protocol you use, a score only means something relative to a trivial baseline such as random guessing or always predicting the majority class; a model that cannot beat it is worthless. Finally, training and test sets must be representative of the data.
overview.importance: Baselines are the first sanity check in every project; chapter 6 makes 'beat a simple baseline' an explicit step of the universal workflow (p.213). The concrete baseline numbers for MNIST, IMDb and Reuters tie this abstract advice to the models already built.
learning_objectives: Describe iterated K-fold validation with shuffling and compute its cost (P x K models)
Explain why a validation score must be compared to a common-sense baseline
Compute baseline accuracies: random classifier for balanced classes, majority-class classifier for imbalanced ones
Recall the book's baselines for MNIST (0.1), IMDb (0.5) and Reuters (about 0.18-0.19)
State the data-representativeness requirement for evaluation splits
prerequisites: The MNIST, IMDb and Reuters examples of chapters 2 and 4

summary:
**Iterated K-fold validation with shuffling** is the third protocol. It is for when you have relatively little data and need the most precise evaluation possible; the author reports it has been extremely helpful in Kaggle competitions. You run K-fold validation several times, reshuffling the data before each K-way split, and the final score is the average over all runs. With `P` iterations you train and evaluate `P * K` models, which can be very expensive.

**5.2.2 Beating a common-sense baseline.** Training a deep model is likened to launching a rocket in a parallel world: you cannot see the manifold-learning process happening in thousands of dimensions, and your only feedback is validation metrics, an "altitude meter". The crucial question is whether you have left the ground at all: is 15% accuracy any good? Before working on a dataset, pick a trivial baseline to beat; crossing it shows the model is genuinely using information in the input to make predictions that generalize. The baseline can be a random classifier or the simplest non-ML technique you can imagine. Examples: MNIST, validation accuracy above 0.1 (random over 10 classes); IMDb, above 0.5; Reuters, about 0.18-0.19 because of class imbalance; a binary problem with 90%/10% classes, 0.9, achieved by always predicting the majority class. A baseline is essential for problems nobody has solved before: if you cannot beat a trivial solution, your model is worthless, perhaps because the model is wrong or because the problem cannot be approached with ML at all.

**5.2.3 Things to keep in mind** opens a checklist. The first item, **data representativeness**, requires training and test sets both to be representative of the data; its digit-classification example (data sorted by class) continues on p.177.

paragraphs.excerpt: This one is for situations in which you have relatively little data
paragraphs.what_it_says: Iterated K-fold with shuffling: for little data and maximum precision. Apply K-fold several times, reshuffling before each K-way split; the final score is the average over runs. With P iterations you train P*K models, which can be very expensive. The author has found it very helpful in Kaggle competitions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Plain K-fold still depends on one particular partition into K blocks. Reshuffling and repeating averages over many partitions, so the estimate depends even less on luck.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: In competitions, small differences between configurations decide rankings, and a single K-fold run may be too noisy to distinguish them; but the cost multiplies by P.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Final score = (1/P) * sum over runs of (1/K) * sum over folds of s_{p,k} = average of all P*K fold scores.

terminology.meaning: One complete K-fold run with its own shuffle.
A platform hosting machine-learning competitions (discussed later in the book).

connections: p.175: Plain K-fold and its averaged score.
p.205: Chapter 6 recommends iterated K-fold 'for performing highly accurate model evaluation when little data is available'.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces common-sense baselines as the last thing to know besides evaluation protocols.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Protocols tell you how to measure reliably; baselines tell you how to interpret the measurement.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without a reference point, a reliable number can still be meaningless.

paragraphs.excerpt: Training a deep learning model is a bit like pressing a button
paragraphs.what_it_says: Training is like launching a rocket in a parallel world you cannot see or hear. The manifold-learning process happens in thousands of dimensions and would be uninterpretable even projected to 3D. Your only feedback is validation metrics, like an altitude meter on an invisible rocket.
paragraphs.what_it_means: You cannot inspect learning directly; you can only read numbers. So you must know what those numbers would be if nothing had been learned.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It justifies treating evaluation metrics, and their reference points, as the primary instrument of model development.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 'Manifold learning' refers back to section 5.1.2, where generalization is explained as learning to interpolate along the latent manifold of the data.

terminology.meaning: The model progressively fitting a smooth mapping that captures the low-dimensional structure (latent manifold) of the training data (section 5.1.2).

connections: p.167: Section 5.1.2 on the nature of generalization and the manifold hypothesis.

paragraphs.excerpt: A particularly important point is to be able to tell whether you're
paragraphs.what_it_says: The key question is whether you are getting off the ground at all: what altitude did you start at? Is 15% accuracy good? Always pick a trivial baseline to beat before starting. Crossing it means the model uses input information to make predictions that generalize. The baseline can be a random classifier or the simplest non-ML technique.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A baseline is the score you get for free. The model's value is the margin above it, not the raw score. 15% accuracy is a strong result on a 100-class problem and a failure on a 2-class problem.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first milestone ('statistical power') in the workflow of chapter 6: before scaling up or regularizing, verify you beat the trivial solution.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: common baselines are uniform random guessing (accuracy 1/C for C classes), majority-class prediction (accuracy = frequency of the most common class), and for regression, predicting the training mean.

terminology.meaning: Performance of a strategy that uses no learned information from the inputs.
A classifier that guesses labels at random.

connections: p.213: Chapter 6 summary lists 'Achieve statistical power: beat a simple baseline'.

paragraphs.excerpt: For instance, in the MNIST digit-classification example, a simple baseline would be
paragraphs.what_it_says: Baselines: MNIST, validation accuracy greater than 0.1 (random classifier); IMDb, greater than 0.5; Reuters, around 0.18-0.19 due to class imbalance. With 90% class A and 10% class B, always predicting A gives 0.9 accuracy, which you must beat.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The baseline depends on the number of classes and their distribution. Balanced 10-class MNIST: 1/10. Balanced binary IMDb: 1/2. Reuters' 46 topics are imbalanced, so the random-guessing baseline is higher than 1/46. With strong imbalance, the majority-class predictor sets a high bar.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Imbalanced problems hide failure: 90% accuracy sounds great but may be no better than a constant prediction.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a random classifier that guesses labels with the same frequencies as the data has expected accuracy $\sum_c p_c^2$. For Reuters this is what was computed empirically in chapter 4 by shuffling labels; with a 90/10 split it gives 0.82, while always predicting the majority class gives 0.9.

terminology.meaning: Some classes are much more frequent than others.
Always predicting the most frequent class.

connections: p.144: The Reuters newswire classification example (46 topics) of section 4.2.
p.135: The IMDb binary classification example.

paragraphs.excerpt: Having a common sense baseline you can refer to is essential when
paragraphs.what_it_says: A baseline is essential for problems no one has solved before. If you cannot beat a trivial solution, your model is worthless; perhaps the model is wrong or the problem cannot be approached with ML. Go back to the drawing board.
paragraphs.what_it_means: On well-known benchmarks you can compare with published results; on new problems the baseline is the only reference you have.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Failing to beat the baseline is a decisive signal to rethink the model, the data, or whether ML fits the problem, rather than tuning further.
connections: p.205: Chapter 6 workflow: developing a model starts with a protocol and a baseline.

paragraphs.excerpt: Data representativeness—You want both your training set and test set to be
paragraphs.what_it_says: First checklist item: training and test sets must both be representative of the data at hand. The example starts: classifying digit images from an array where samples are (continued on p.177: ordered by class).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A split must preserve the distribution of the data in each part. If the array is sorted, a naive first-80%/last-20% split gives training and test sets with different classes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A non-representative test set gives a meaningless estimate; this is why Listings 5.5 and 5.6 shuffle before splitting.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: stratified splitting keeps class proportions equal across splits.

terminology.meaning: Having roughly the same distribution as the whole dataset (and, ideally, as production data).

concepts.name: Iterated K-fold validation with shuffling
concepts.definition: Running K-fold validation P times, reshuffling before each split, and averaging all scores.
concepts.intuition: Repeat the rotation with different shuffles so no single partition dominates.
concepts.technical: P*K models trained and evaluated; final score is the mean of the P K-fold averages.
concepts.significance: The most precise of the three protocols for small data, and the most expensive.
concepts.misconception: That it is always worth it; on large datasets simple hold-out suffices (p.205).

concepts.name: Common-sense baseline
concepts.definition: The performance of a trivial strategy (random guessing, majority class, simplest non-ML technique) that a model must beat.
concepts.intuition: The starting altitude of the rocket.
concepts.technical: For balanced C-class problems, 1/C accuracy; for imbalanced ones, the majority-class frequency is a stronger bar.
concepts.significance: Tells you whether the model is learning anything that generalizes.
concepts.misconception: That high accuracy is automatically good; on 90/10 data, 0.9 is free.

concepts.name: Class imbalance
concepts.definition: Unequal class frequencies in a dataset.
concepts.intuition: If most emails are not spam, saying 'not spam' every time is usually right.
concepts.technical: Raises trivial-baseline accuracy above 1/C and makes accuracy alone misleading.
concepts.significance: Explains the Reuters baseline of 0.18-0.19 and the 0.9 baseline in the 90/10 example.
concepts.misconception: That a random baseline is always 1/C.

concepts.name: Data representativeness
concepts.definition: Training and test sets should each reflect the distribution of the data at hand.
concepts.intuition: A sample should look like the population.
concepts.technical: Usually achieved by random shuffling before splitting (except for temporal data, p.177).
concepts.significance: Without it, the test score estimates performance on a different distribution.
concepts.example: Digits sorted by class: first 80% contains only classes 0-7 (p.177).
concepts.misconception: That any split of the right size will do.

math.title: Cost and score of iterated K-fold
math.source_text: The final score is the average of the scores obtained at each run of K-fold validation. ... you end up training and evaluating P * K models

variables.meaning: Number of iterations (K-fold runs, each with its own shuffle)
Validation score of fold k in run p

math.operations: Nested averaging; multiplication for the model count.
math.purpose: Quantifies both the estimate and its compute cost.
math.interpretation: Precision grows with P, cost grows linearly with P.
math.intuition: More shuffles, more independent views of the same small dataset.
math.numerical_example: K = 5, P = 4: 20 models. If one training run takes 3 minutes, one configuration costs an hour.

math.title: Trivial-baseline accuracies
math.source_text: MNIST ... greater than 0.1 (random classifier); IMDB ... greater than 0.5 ... 90% of samples belong to class A ... always predicts A already achieves 0.9

variables.meaning: Fraction of samples belonging to class c

math.purpose: Gives the threshold a model must exceed.
math.interpretation: For balanced classes both are equal to 1/C; imbalance raises the majority baseline.
math.intuition: Guessing gets you 1/C; always betting on the favourite gets you its frequency.
math.numerical_example: MNIST C = 10: 0.1. IMDb C = 2: 0.5. 90/10 binary: majority baseline 0.9.

deeper.title: Where does the Reuters 0.18-0.19 come from?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: a classifier that draws random labels with the data's own class frequencies is correct with probability $\sum_c p_c^2$ (the chance that the prediction and the truth fall in the same class). For a uniform distribution this is $1/C$; imbalance makes it larger. The Reuters labels are dominated by a few topics, which is why the book quotes roughly 0.18-0.19 instead of $1/46 \approx 0.022$. For a 90/10 binary split the same formula gives $0.81 + 0.01 = 0.82$, while always predicting A gives 0.9, so the majority baseline is the stronger bar.

deeper.title: Baselines beyond classification
deeper.body: Beyond the book: for regression, predict the training-set mean (or median for MAE); for forecasting, predict that tomorrow equals today (persistence). The book uses a common-sense forecast of this kind later in its time-series chapter. The principle is the same: compute what you get with zero learning.

deeper.title: The invisible rocket
deeper.body: The book's analogy (source: book) is a rocket you cannot see, with only an altimeter. Extending it: a reading of 1,000 m means nothing if the launch pad was on a 1,200 m plateau. The baseline is the height of the launch pad.

misconceptions.claim: 90% accuracy is always a good result.
misconceptions.correction: On a 90/10 binary problem, always predicting the majority class already gives 0.9.

misconceptions.claim: The random baseline for Reuters is 1/46.
misconceptions.correction: Because of class imbalance, the book gives about 0.18-0.19.

misconceptions.claim: Iterated K-fold is the best default protocol.
misconceptions.correction: It costs P x K trainings; it is for small data when maximum precision is needed. Hold-out works in most cases (p.205).

earlier.note: K-fold validation, which iterated K-fold repeats.
Hold-out validation and the forward reference to baselines.
Manifold view of generalization referred to by the rocket analogy.

later.note: Representativeness example, arrow of time, redundancy.
Protocol choice in the universal workflow.
Beat a simple baseline as a workflow step.

takeaways: Iterated K-fold: repeat K-fold P times with reshuffling, average; costs P x K models.
Always pick a trivial baseline before training; a score is only meaningful relative to it.
Baselines: MNIST 0.1, IMDb 0.5, Reuters about 0.18-0.19, 90/10 binary 0.9.
If you cannot beat the baseline, rethink the model or whether ML applies.
Training and test sets must be representative of the data.

questions.question: You run iterated K-fold with K = 5 and P = 3. How many models are trained and evaluated?
questions.explanation: The page states the count is P * K = 3 * 5.

questions.question: A binary dataset has 90% class A. Which validation accuracy must a model beat to be useful?
questions.explanation: Always predicting A gives 0.9. 0.5 would be the balanced-binary baseline, 0.1 is MNIST's, and 1.0 is perfection, not a baseline.

questions.question: Why is the Reuters baseline about 0.18-0.19 rather than 1/46?
questions.answer: Because the 46 classes are imbalanced: a few topics are much more frequent, so random guessing that follows the class distribution is right more often than 1/46.
questions.explanation: The page attributes the figure to class imbalance.

questions.question: What does it tell you when your model cannot beat a common-sense baseline, according to the book?
questions.answer: That the model is worthless as is: either you are using the wrong model, or the problem may not be approachable with machine learning; go back to the drawing board.
questions.explanation: Direct from the last paragraph of section 5.2.2.

questions.question: Which situation is iterated K-fold validation designed for?
options: Huge datasets where training is slow
Relatively little data and a need for very precise evaluation
questions.answer: Relatively little data and a need for very precise evaluation
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sentence. For huge datasets hold-out suffices; time series must not be shuffled (p.177); duplicates are a separate pitfall (p.177).

questions.question: Explain the rocket analogy: what does the altitude meter correspond to, and why does the starting altitude matter?
questions.answer: The altimeter is the validation metric, your only window on an unobservable high-dimensional learning process. The starting altitude is the trivial baseline: without it you cannot tell whether a reading like 15% accuracy means you have taken off.
questions.explanation: From the second and third printed paragraphs of 5.2.2.

questions.question: For a project you know, write down the trivial baseline before thinking about the model. What is it and how would you compute it?
questions.answer: Answers vary: e.g., majority class frequency for classification, training mean for regression, yesterday's value for forecasting.
questions.explanation: The book advises picking the baseline before you start working with the dataset.
